newsitem.title: UK: Sterling safe even if UK holds rates - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sterling safe even if UK holds rates - analysts.

text.p: Sterling has stumbled in recent days as expectations fade of a rise in interest rates after Wednesday's monetary meeting, but its slip should not become a slide even if rates stay put this week, analysts said.
A new survey showing British retail sales growth slowed again in December came hot on the heels of an unexpected fall in November manufacturing output and subdued producer price data for last month.
"Expectations are shifting towards no (rate) hike and that explains a lot of the slackening off in sterling in the last few days," James Barty at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said on Tuesday.

"Because the decision is quite finely balanced, though, I don't think a "no move' is fully priced in and you might see sterling come back a little bit more if they don't raise rates," added Barty, who is a UK economist at DMG in London.

British base rates were increased by a quarter-point to six percent on October 30, 1996, and with data consistently pointing to economic strength, sterling rallied sharply as the market banked on further rate hikes.
But the recent softer-toned data were seen as offering ammunition to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, should he wish to fight Bank of England calls for credit tightening.

If rates stay steady after Wednesday's monthly meeting between Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George, expectations that a hike has been postponed rather than cancelled should keep sterling underpinned, analysts said.

"Possibly there'll be a bit of a pullback...but I don't see a major fall, partly because the next meeting is only three weeks later so people will simply be focusing their attention further on," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Sterling stood at 2.6555 marks at 1130 GMT, down from the January 9 high of 2.6767, which represented a gain of more than 16 percent since August and its best level since September 1992.
Against the dollar, the pound had climbed over 15 percent since May to scale a four-year peak of $1.7163 on December 31, but has since eased to trade at $1.6725 by midsession Tuesday.

Clarke may want to keep rates steady for now so he can see fourth-quarter GDP data -- due on January 27 -- before acting, analysts suggested. Weak economic growth numbers would deal a further blow to hopes of monetary tightening.
Though dented, expectations of a rate hike this week are not dead. All the same, economists said sterling should welcome tightening and at least make good recent losses.

The Chancellor's fondness for surprising the market -- as on October 30 -- and for being seen to be "ahead of the curve' may mean he chooses to move this week, analysts said. He will also be reluctant to upset home owners by tightening too close to the forthcoming election, which must be held by May.
"The market isn't expecting it now, so he could look tough at very little cost," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy here.
Market watchers have not ruled out the possibility that Clarke may not touch rates at all before the election, but believe even that may not worry the pound unduly.

"Even if rates don't go up, or only rise modestly in the year as we expect, there's still a fairly decent interest rate differential between the UK and the Continent, where the bias towards monetary policy will be downwards," said HSBC's Loynes.
Britain should also outshine fellow European Union states as they tighten their belts ahead of monetary union, he added.
But CIBC's Coleman warned that political concerns could take the gloss off sterling, saying history showed the currency suffered a vulnerable period ahead of elections.
"Sterling's had a great run," he said. "But we do have some political concerns to get through."
